newsitem.title: JAPAN: Dollar to march upward despite intervention scare.
newsitem.headline: Dollar to march upward despite intervention scare.

text.p: The dollar is likely to continue its upward march against the yen, traders say, with few expecting the Bank of Japan to openly intervene in the market when fundamental factors are driving the Japanese currency lower.
The dollar rose to the key level of 125 yen on Monday, its highest level since February 1993 and up from 124.30 at the New York close on Friday.
Dealers said that Japanese monetary authorities are increasingly worried that the weak yen will re-ignite trade friction with the United States.
But they say that given the jittery state of markets globally, especially Wall Street, they do not want to risk a spat that could spark a market fallout.

After the global stock market crash of October 1987, some analysts said the rout was caused in part by a spat between Alan Greenspan, then the new chairman of the Federal Reserve, and his foreign counterparts over interest rates and the level of the dollar.

"It would be difficult for Japan to take action that will directly lower the value of the dollar amid the unstable U.S. financial markets," said Shinichiro Maruyama, head of spot trading at Industrial Bank of Japan (IBJ) Ltd.
A falling dollar would make U.S. assets less attractive and could prompt a pullout from the U.S. market.
Wall Street is already nervous about whether the long-running bull market is coming to an end and some experts say any trigger could cause a tumble in prices.
The Dow Jones industrial average ended at 6,526.07 on Friday, nearly eight percent off its peak of 7,112.10.
A rise in wage costs in U.S. labour market has fanned fears that the Federal Reserve may again tighten credit.
Interest rate gaps of 10-year government bonds between Japan and the United States have widened to around 4.8 percent from 4.35 percent before the Fed pushed up rates in late March.
Traders said that with such fundamental factors favouring the dollar, it would take massive levels of intervention to push the yen back up.
"Unless the Bank of Japan is determined to guide the dollar down to around 115 yen through massive dollar selling, intervention would be ineffective," said IBJ's Maruyama.
He added that lukewarm intervention would result in nudging the dollar down to around 123 yen, giving investors good chances to bargain-hunt for dollars cheaply.
A senior trader at a leading Japanese bank said overwhelming dollar buying interest by Japanese investors is likely to push the dollar up past the key level of 125 yen.

U.S. funds operators joined forces to buy up dollars against the yen while Asian operators including central banks seemed to be interested in selling dollars on rises above 125 yen, said the Japanese bank dealer.

He said there is a possibility that the BOJ will discreetly sell dollars for yen via monetary authorities in Singapore and Hong Kong. In February 1996, they agreed with Japan to act on behalf of Japan to prevent currency fluctuations.
Dealers said that unless the U.S. takes concerted action with Japan to halt the dollar's further rise, single-handed intervention by Japan would have only limited impact.

U.S. Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin Rubin, who stopped off here on Friday before a weekend meeting of Asia-Pacific finance ministers in the Philippines, repeatedly stressed the importance of Japan avoiding a resurgence of its trade surplus by promoting strong demand at home for its products.
But he said the use of currency rates was not the answer to solving the trade surplus problem.
